pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 2: Algorithm

Computers process input data by evaluating expressions in a strict order and storing results in variables. In this unit you will apply BODMAS as a computer does, and draw flowcharts that solve real problems in your environment.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.4.2.1** Analyse the correct step-by-step procedure in solving any real-world problem.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.4.2.1.1** Apply variables, expressions, assignment statements and operator precedence order (BODMAS) to process and store numbers and text.
- **B8.4.2.1.2** Describe and use sequence, selection and iteration statements; understand variables vs constants and naming conventions.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 13.1 Variables, Expressions, Assignment and BODMAS
- 13.2 Sequence, Selection and Iteration with Flowcharts

**Core competencies developed:** Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (CP5.5, CP6.5).

pages.title: Variables, Expressions, Assignment and BODMAS
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.4.2.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- compute expressions following operator precedence;
- show how computers process input to produce output;
- store numbers and text in variables.
**BODMAS** stands for **B**rackets, **O**f (orders/powers), **D**ivision, **M**ultiplication, **A**ddition, **S**ubtraction. Division and multiplication have equal priority and are worked **left to right**; so are addition and subtraction. Programming languages follow the same rules.
> ✏️ **Worked example — How the computer evaluates result = 20 - 3 ∗ (2 + 4) / 9 + 2 ∗∗ 2**
1. Brackets: (2 + 4) = 6 → 20 - 3 ∗ 6 / 9 + 2 ∗∗ 2
2. Orders (powers): 2 ∗ 2 = 4 → `20 - 3 6 / 9 + 4`
3. Division and multiplication, left to right: 3 ∗ 6 = 18; 18 / 9 = 2 → 20 - 2 + 4
4. Addition and subtraction, left to right: 20 − 2 = 18; 18 + 4 = 22
5. Assignment: the value **22.0** is stored in the variable result (Python shows a decimal because of the division).
> ✏️ **Worked example — A program that processes input data**
name = input("Enter your name: ") # text stored in a variable
test = float(input("Class test (out of 40): "))
exam = float(input("Exam (out of 60): "))
total = test + exam # assignment of an expression
percent_test = test / 40 ∗ 100
print(name, "scored", total, "out of 100")
**Input:** Kojo, 32, 51 → **Output:** Kojo scored 83.0 out of 100

pages.title: Sequence, Selection and Iteration with Flowcharts
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.4.2.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- draw the four basic flowchart symbols;
- arrange symbols to solve a real problem;
- choose appropriate naming conventions for variables and constants.
[[fig:c8-f18|Figure 17: The four basic flowchart symbols]]
A **flowchart** is a diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols connected by **flow lines** (arrows). Flowcharts show **sequence** (one box after another), **selection** (a decision diamond with Yes/No branches) and **iteration** (a flow line that loops back to an earlier step).
[[fig:c8-f19|Figure 18: Flowchart for preparing land for a maize farm]]
> ✏️ **Worked example — Reading the maize-farm flowchart**
- **Sequence:** clear the bush → plough → make ridges.
- **Selection:** “Soil fertile?” If **No**, add manure; if **Yes**, continue.
- **Iteration:** “Weeds still present?” If **Yes**, apply herbicide/weed again and check again, repeating until there are no weeds.
## Variables vs constants and naming conventions
| **Convention** | **Example** | **Typical use** |
|---|---|---|
| snake_case | total_score | Variables in Python |
| camelCase | totalScore | Variables in JavaScript, Java, Scratch |
| PascalCase | TotalScore | Names of classes |
| UPPER_CASE | MAX_SCORE, PI | Constants |

pages.title: Sequence, Selection and Iteration with Flowcharts (continued)
pages.body:
- Choose names that describe the data: farm_size_acres not f.
- Be consistent: use one style throughout a program.
- Use constants for values that should never change (e.g. HOURS_IN_DAY = 24) so they cannot be changed by mistake and are easy to update in one place.
> 🧪 **Activity — Your own flowchart**
Identify a real problem in your environment (e.g. fetching water, preparing for an exam, crossing a busy road safely, running a school canteen). Draw a flowchart that uses all four symbols and includes at least one decision and one loop. Exchange with a partner and check whether the logic works.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Evaluate step by step: 18 / 3 + 2 (5 − 1) ∗ 2.
2. Draw the four basic flowchart symbols and state the use of each.
3. Draw a flowchart that inputs two numbers and outputs the larger one.
4. Draw a flowchart that prints the 5 times table from 5 × 1 to 5 × 12.
